Lecture 3: The Cell Membrane
Objectives
• Describe the structure of the plasma membrane
• Compare passive and active transport
• Explain the role of membrane proteins

Functions of the membrane
• Barrier between the cell and its environment
• Selective permeability
• Cell signalling
• Cell adhesion
• Cell recognition

Fluid Mosaic Model
• Phospholipid bilayer with embedded proteins
• Cholesterol regulates membrane fluidity
• Carbohydrates form the glycocalyx used for recognition
• Proteins can move laterally within the bilayer

Transport across the membrane
Passive transport: movement down a concentration gradient without energy
Active transport: movement against the gradient using ATP
Osmosis: diffusion of water across a semipermeable membrane
Facilitated diffusion: uses channel or carrier proteins

Types of membrane proteins
• Integral proteins span the bilayer
• Peripheral proteins attach to the surface
• Receptors bind signalling molecules
• Channels allow ions to pass
• Carriers change shape to move solutes

Sodium-potassium pump
1. Three Na+ ions bind inside the cell
2. ATP phosphorylates the pump
3. The pump changes shape and releases Na+ outside
4. Two K+ ions bind outside and are released inside
Result: a steep sodium gradient is maintained across the membrane
notes_en: The plasma membrane separates the cell from its surroundings. It is made mainly of phospholipids and proteins. The membrane controls which substances enter and leave the cell.

Diffusion occurs when particles move from a region of high concentration to a region of low concentration. Temperature increases the rate of diffusion because particles move faster. Larger molecules diffuse more slowly than small molecules.

Osmosis is the movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane. A hypotonic solution causes cells to swell, whereas a hypertonic solution causes cells to shrink. Red blood cells burst in pure water because water enters by osmosis.

Active transport requires energy from ATP. The sodium-potassium pump moves three sodium ions out and two potassium ions in. This unequal movement creates an electrical gradient across the membrane of about -70 mV in neurons.

dense_en: Cardiac output is the volume of blood pumped by the heart per minute. It equals stroke volume multiplied by heart rate. Exercise increases cardiac output because both stroke volume and heart rate rise. Preload is the stretch of the ventricular wall before contraction. Afterload is the resistance the ventricle must overcome to eject blood.

Blood pressure depends on cardiac output and peripheral resistance. Vasoconstriction increases resistance and therefore raises pressure. The baroreceptor reflex detects changes in arterial pressure and adjusts heart rate. A rise in pressure leads to a reduction in heart rate through the vagus nerve.
lecture_en:
Cardiac Cycle Overview
The cardiac cycle is the sequence of electrical and mechanical events during one heartbeat.
Systole: the contraction phase in which the ventricles eject blood into the arteries.
Diastole: the relaxation phase in which the ventricles fill with blood from the atria.
Stroke volume: the volume of blood ejected by one ventricle during a single contraction.
Cardiac output: the volume of blood pumped by each ventricle per minute.
A rise in stroke volume leads to a higher cardiac output at the same heart rate.
Normal resting heart rate in adults is about 70 bpm in healthy individuals.
Phases of the cycle include isovolumetric contraction, ejection, isovolumetric relaxation and filling.

Cardiac Conduction System
The sinoatrial node is the natural pacemaker that initiates each heartbeat.
The atrioventricular node delays the impulse so the atria can finish contracting.
Purkinje fibres: specialised conducting cells that spread the impulse rapidly through the ventricles.
Impulse conduction proceeds in a fixed order:
1. The sinoatrial node generates the impulse in the right atrium.
2. The impulse crosses the atria and reaches the atrioventricular node.
3. The bundle of His carries the impulse into the interventricular septum.
4. Purkinje fibres distribute the impulse to the ventricular myocardium.
Damage to the atrioventricular node results in delayed conduction between atria and ventricles.
The atrioventricular node delays the impulse for about 100 ms before it passes on.

Cardiac Action Potential
The ventricular action potential has five phases that depend on ion movements across the membrane.
Depolarization: the rapid influx of sodium ions that raises the membrane potential.
Plateau phase: the period of sustained calcium entry that prolongs the contraction.
Repolarization: the efflux of potassium ions that restores the resting membrane potential.
Prolonged calcium entry causes the long plateau seen in ventricular myocytes.
The resting membrane potential of a ventricular myocyte is about -90 mV in healthy tissue.
Ion channels involved include voltage-gated sodium channels, L-type calcium channels and potassium channels.

Blood Pressure Regulation
Blood pressure is the force exerted by circulating blood on the walls of the arteries.
Baroreceptors: stretch-sensitive sensory endings in the aortic arch and carotid sinus that monitor arterial pressure.
Mean arterial pressure: the average pressure in the arteries during one complete cardiac cycle.
A fall in arterial pressure leads to increased sympathetic activity through the baroreceptor reflex.
Increased sympathetic activity causes faster heart rate and stronger contraction of the heart.
Normal systolic pressure in healthy adults is around 120 mmHg at rest.
Short-term regulation mechanisms include the baroreceptor reflex, chemoreceptor reflex and hormonal control.

Heart Sounds
The first heart sound is produced by closure of the atrioventricular valves at the start of systole.
The second heart sound is produced by closure of the semilunar valves at the start of diastole.
Murmur: an abnormal sound caused by turbulent blood flow across a narrowed or leaking valve.
Valve stenosis leads to turbulent flow and a characteristic murmur during blood ejection.
Auscultation areas include the aortic area, pulmonic area, tricuspid area and mitral area.

Electrocardiogram
Electrocardiogram: a recording of the electrical activity of the heart from electrodes on the skin.
P wave: the deflection that represents atrial depolarization.
QRS complex: the deflection that represents ventricular depolarization.
T wave: the deflection that represents ventricular repolarization.
A prolonged PR interval results in slow conduction through the atrioventricular node.
The normal QRS duration is less than 120 ms in healthy adults.
Standard recording leads include the limb leads, the augmented leads and the chest leads.

Coronary Circulation
Coronary arteries: the vessels that supply oxygenated blood to the heart muscle itself.
Coronary perfusion occurs mainly during diastole when the ventricular wall is relaxed.
A blocked coronary artery leads to reduced oxygen supply and ischaemic damage to the myocardium.
Atherosclerosis: the build-up of fatty plaques inside the walls of arteries that narrows the lumen.
Risk factors include smoking, hypertension, high cholesterol and diabetes.
Plaque formation proceeds in a fixed order:
1. Endothelial injury allows lipoproteins to enter the vessel wall.
2. Macrophages engulf the lipoproteins and become foam cells.
3. Smooth muscle cells migrate and form a fibrous cap over the lesion.
4. The cap may rupture and trigger thrombus formation inside the vessel.

Heart Failure
Heart failure: a condition in which the heart cannot pump enough blood to meet the needs of the body.
Preload: the stretch of the ventricular wall at the end of filling before contraction.
Afterload: the resistance that the ventricle must overcome to eject blood into the arteries.
Increased afterload causes higher workload and eventual thickening of the ventricular wall.
Reduced contractility results in a lower ejection fraction and congestion in the lungs.
Normal ejection fraction in healthy adults is about 60 percent of the end-diastolic volume.
Typical symptoms include breathlessness, fatigue, ankle swelling and reduced exercise tolerance.
